cards.heading: Weak-to-strong generalization: setup
cards.question: What is the weak-to-strong generalization (W2S) research setup?
cards.answer: A weak model is trained on labeled data; its pseudo-labels then train a strong model on unlabeled data. The question is how much of the strong model's latent capability survives supervision by a weaker teacher — a proxy for humans overseeing superhuman AI.

cards.heading: Performance Gap Recovery formula
cards.question: How is Performance Gap Recovery (PGR) calculated in weak-to-strong generalization?
cards.answer: PGR = (transfer accuracy − weak accuracy) / (strong accuracy − weak accuracy), where transfer accuracy is the strong student trained on weak labels, weak accuracy is the weak teacher, and strong accuracy is a strong ceiling trained on ground truth.

cards.heading: Interpreting PGR 0 vs PGR 1
cards.question: What do PGR values of 0 and 1 mean in weak-to-strong generalization?
cards.answer: PGR 0 means the student was capped at the weak teacher's level; PGR 1 means the student fully recovered ground-truth performance despite noisy weak supervision.

cards.heading: W2S baseline method families
cards.question: What are the three baseline method families used to improve weak-to-strong generalization?
cards.answer: Training only on confident weak labels (confidence filtering), using strong-model critiques to improve the labels, and unsupervised elicitation that draws the answer out of the strong model rather than teaching it.

cards.heading: Why W2S is useful as a framing
cards.question: What is the value of the weak-to-strong generalization framing for alignment research?
cards.answer: It converts a philosophical worry — humans supervising AI smarter than themselves — into a measured, quantifiable question on ordinary benchmarks.
